title: The Tape Needs Two Copies
subtitle: A home video is more than a file to digitize. A thoughtful transfer preserves the footage—and the names, places and context that help a family understand it later.
imageAlt: A couple and an older relative sit together at a table with a VHS cassette, a handwritten note and a laptop showing a paused family video.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene of a couple and an older family member preparing one VHS tape at a kitchen table: the cassette and its label in the foreground, a notebook open to a few identifying details, and a laptop nearby but not playing the tape.
body: Start with one tape, not the whole shelf

A box of home videos can feel like a project with no natural finish line. Make the first goal smaller: choose one cassette and find out what the family already knows about it. That keeps the work manageable, and it gives the people who recognize the voices or places a chance to contribute before those details become harder to recall.

Invite a couple and an older relative—or any family members who want to take part—to look at the cassette together. No one needs to supply a complete history. The label may offer a year, a holiday, a surname or only a few words. Treat those clues as a starting point, not a verdict. One person might recognize a room; another might know which branch of the family used a nickname. Even partial context can make a video easier to find and meaningful to future viewers.

This is cultural record-keeping on a household scale. A recording can show more than the event its maker intended to capture: the way people spoke, what a room looked like, who was present and which details seemed ordinary enough not to explain. The National Archives recommends recording descriptive information such as a video’s title, date, location or occasion. That information belongs alongside the image, not only in someone’s memory [1].
Write down what is known—and what is not

Before arranging a transfer, make a short note about the tape. Copy its label as written, then add what the family is reasonably confident about: names, approximate dates, places and occasions. If a detail is uncertain, mark it that way. “Probably the reunion at Aunt Lee’s house, around 1992” is more useful and honest than turning a guess into a precise caption.

A simple record might include the tape’s current label, a working title, the people who helped identify it, any date or location clues, and questions that remain. Keep it plain. The purpose is not to produce a formal family history; it is to give the digital files enough context that someone can recognize them later. If the tape contains several occasions, note that the footage may cover more than one event rather than forcing it into a single description.

Share the note with the people involved and let them correct, add or decline to identify anything. Names and family relationships can be sensitive, and participation should be voluntary. A family can choose not to include private details or to restrict who receives a copy. Good description makes a record more findable without requiring every story to be made public.
Do not test the tape in a questionable player

The impulse to put the cassette into an old VCR “just to see what’s on it” is understandable, but playback is not risk-free. The National Archives warns that each playback can put audiovisual material at risk of damage [2]. A visibly compromised tape should not be tested at home.

The same caution applies when a machine has been stored for years or its condition is uncertain. A tape can be affected by the equipment used to play it, and a successful picture on a television does not establish that the transfer is complete or suitable for long-term preservation. If the cassette looks damaged, has debris, or raises concerns, pause and ask a qualified transfer provider or an audiovisual preservation specialist what to do. Do not clean, open or repair it as a first step.

This is a good point to make the decision together: is the tape in a condition that seems appropriate to send for assessment, and who will contact a provider? The family does not need to diagnose the cassette. The useful action is to limit unnecessary handling and get advice before risking another playback.
Ask for two different kinds of copy

When contacting a transfer service, ask explicitly about two deliverables: a preservation copy intended to support long-term keeping, and an access copy that is convenient to play and share. The National Archives distinguishes these purposes; a file that works easily on a laptop is not automatically a preservation-quality master [1][2]. The formats and options available vary, so ask the provider to explain what they can supply rather than assuming that “digital” means one particular thing.

Useful questions include: What will the preservation and viewing files be? Can the descriptive note travel with the files? How will the files be named? What does delivery include, and how will the family receive them? Ask whether the original cassette will be returned and whether any charges or choices depend on the tape’s condition. These questions help make the result understandable before the transfer begins.

Give the provider the written context, including uncertainty. A title such as “Family gathering, possible summer 1992” is more informative than “Tape 1,” while still leaving room for correction. If there are several clips or occasions, ask how they will be represented. A clear handoff reduces the chance that a useful file arrives with no clue about what it contains.
Name the files for people who were not there

Once the files arrive, use names that make sense outside the moment of transfer. A consistent pattern can combine an approximate date, an occasion or location, and a short identifier: for example, “1992-approx_family-reunion_tape-01.” Avoid putting sensitive personal details in a filename if the file may be shared broadly. Keep a separate note when fuller context belongs somewhere more private.

Save the description in a small text document alongside the video, or in another simple place the family can find. Include the original cassette label, the working title, what is known about the date and location, who contributed information, and any unresolved questions. A future viewer should not have to infer everything from a folder called “old videos.” A Library of Congress post about WITNESS’s digital-video archiving guide describes organization, cataloging, storage and integrity checks as parts of a preservation workflow—not afterthoughts [3].

Use the viewing file for ordinary watching and sharing; keep the preservation file clearly identified and avoid treating it as the everyday version. This distinction is practical, not ceremonial. It helps family members know which file is convenient to open and which one should be protected as the best available transfer.
Make a backup before the first family screening

Keep at least one additional copy of the transferred files, stored separately from the first. A file on one computer can be lost if that device fails, is replaced or is misplaced. A second copy on another storage device or in a trusted storage service reduces the risk that a single problem takes out the only digital version. NARA advises maintaining backups and checking digitized files over time [2]; no storage choice should be treated as permanent without review.

Make the arrangement legible: decide who is responsible for the second copy, where it lives, and how the family will know which version is the preservation copy. Keep the descriptive note with each set where possible. At intervals, check that the storage devices are still accessible and that the files open. If the family changes computers or storage services, include the video and its note in the move rather than leaving the context behind.

The first screening can be a shared occasion, but it does not need to become an interrogation. Let people watch before asking for identifications. If someone recognizes a person or place, record the detail afterward and ask whether they want it attached to the family’s copy. A calm viewing gives the recording room to be enjoyed as well as documented.
Leave the story open to correction

A useful home-video record is not a final, authoritative account of a family. The camera chose what to show; the label may be incomplete; viewers may disagree about a date or a name. Preserve that uncertainty rather than polishing it away. Add a later correction with its source, or keep two versions of a detail when the family cannot resolve it. The file’s description can grow as people learn more.

After watching, choose one modest next step: add a newly recognized name to the note, confirm a likely location, or mark the date as approximate. Then decide who should have access to the copies and where the family will keep the written context. This gives the tape a future beyond the transfer appointment: a record that can be found, watched and understood without asking one person to carry every detail in memory.

The aim is not to turn a family evening into an archive project. It is to make one piece of the past easier to encounter on its own terms—without sacrificing the original context for convenience, or pretending that a digital file tells the whole story.
